content: Soil formation (pedogenesis) is a complex, continuous process that transforms parent material into structured soil through physical, chemical, and biological interactions over time. Five main factors influence this process: parent material, climate, topography, biology, and timeâcollectively known as the clorpt equation (Cl=climate, o=organisms, r=relief/topography, p=parent material, t=time). Soil formation begins with weathering of parent materialâthe original geologic substrate that may be residual (bedrock) or transported (glacial till, alluvium, loess). Physical weathering breaks down material through processes like freeze-thaw cycles and root penetration, while chemical weathering alters minerals through reactions like oxidation and hydrolysis. As weathering progresses, organisms colonize the developing substrate. Plants contribute organic matter through leaf litter and root exudates, while animals mix materials through burrowing (bioturbation). Microorganisms decompose organic matter, releasing nutrients and producing humusâstable organic compounds that improve soil structure and fertility. These processes gradually develop distinct soil horizonsâlayers with different physical, chemical, and biological properties. The O horizon contains primarily organic material, the A horizon (topsoil) contains mineral particles mixed with organic matter, the E horizon is a zone of leaching, the B horizon (subsoil) accumulates materials leached from above, and the C horizon consists of partially weathered parent material. Climate strongly influences soil development through temperature and precipitation, which affect weathering rates, organic matter decomposition, and translocation of materials between horizons. Given sufficient time, these processes can transform bare rock into rich, complex soils, though timescales vary from centuries to millennia depending on environmental conditions.

scenario.title: Soil Profile Builder
scenario.content: Students create and develop virtual soil profiles by layering different materials and subjecting them to environmental factors over accelerated time scales. The simulation allows students to select parent materials, adjust climate variables, modify topography, and introduce various organisms to observe their effects on soil formation. The system visualizes microscopic processes like mineral weathering, organic matter decomposition, and clay particle movement alongside macroscopic features like horizon development and structural changes. Interactive tools let students conduct virtual soil tests, measure properties like pH, texture, and organic content throughout the profile, and observe how these properties change over time. Time-lapse features compress centuries of soil development into minutes of simulation time, allowing students to witness gradual processes. Challenge scenarios task students with developing soils for specific purposes (agriculture, construction, habitat restoration) or replicating characteristic soils from different biomes, teaching the applied aspects of soil science.

hypothesis.description: Students will model soil development by manipulating the five soil-forming factors. They will predict how different combinations of parent material, climate, topography, organisms, and time produce various soil types, and explain the processes that create soil horizons and properties.
